title: Given n pairs of parentheses, generate all combinations of well-formed (balanced) parentheses, using backtracking with constraints.
keyPoints: Backtrack with open and close counters: place '(' while open < n, place ')' while close < open.
The close < open invariant prevents any prefix from having more closes than opens, ensuring validity.
The number of valid strings is the nth Catalan number, far smaller than 2^(2n) brute-force candidates.
Use StringBuilder with append-recurse-delete for efficient backtracking without string allocation.
Enforcing validity during construction avoids the exponential waste of generate-then-filter.
This constrained backtracking pattern generalizes to Sudoku, N-Queens, and valid expression generation.

s1_definition.oneliner: Add an opener while openers remain; add a closer only while closers placed are fewer than openers placed; record when both counts reach n.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Generate Parentheses** – produce all well-formed strings of n open and n close parentheses using constrained backtracking.
- **Placement rules** – append `(` while `open < n`; append `)` only while `close < open`.
- **Invariant** – `close < open` keeps every prefix valid, so no post-generation filtering is needed.
- **Count** – results equal the nth Catalan number, which is C(2n,n)/(n+1).
- **Backtracking** – append, recurse, undo (delete last character) at each step.
- **Efficiency** – only valid strings are built, avoiding exponential waste.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India generates all valid nesting patterns for approval workflows. An opener starts a sub-approval and a closer finishes the most recent one. A clerk writes the pattern left to right. She may start a new sub-approval as long as she has not used all her starts, and she may finish one only if there is an unfinished one open. Every pattern she writes is automatically valid.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Backtracking Tree for n=2
  ──────────────────────────

                  ""
                 /
               (
             /   \
           ((     ()
           |      |
          (()    ()(
           |      |
          (())   ()()

  Both leaves are valid strings.
  No invalid prefix was ever built.
```

```text
  Constraint Check at Each Node
  ──────────────────────────────
  open < n  ?  → can place '('
  close < open ?  → can place ')'
  length == 2n ?  → record result
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem generates all well-formed strings of n open and n close parentheses using constrained backtracking. I build the string one character at a time with two counters. I may place an open while the open count is below n, and a close only while the close count is strictly less than the open count. When the string reaches length 2n, it is guaranteed balanced and I record it.

The `close < open` invariant is what prevents invalid prefixes. Because no invalid string is ever started, every leaf of the recursion tree is a valid result, and the total count is the nth Catalan number, which grows far slower than the 2^(2n) brute-force candidates. Using `StringBuilder` with append-recurse-deleteCharAt keeps the backtracking efficient without string allocation overhead.

This constrained backtracking technique, enforcing validity during construction rather than filtering afterward, is a general optimization pattern. It applies equally to Sudoku, N-Queens, and valid expression generation. Recognizing the Catalan number connection signals mathematical maturity to an interviewer.

In my project at the National Bank of India, the approval-rule builder used this to enumerate every valid nesting template for nested approval workflows. Each template was valid by construction, so the governance team reviewed only well-formed structures without wading through nonsensical patterns.

Remember one sentence: place an open while budget remains, place a close only while closes trail opens, and every string built is valid without any filtering.
